title: Spike: prove the UNO+WiFi R3 (ESP8266) can run the IR sniffer/blaster role
description: Owner has a UNO+WiFi R3 ATmega328P+ESP8266 CH340 (4MB flash ESP8266, external antenna) sitting around; if its ESP8266 half can run ESPHome remote_receiver/remote_transmitter, it becomes a candidate for the enclosed (Altoids tin) build where the Feather's PCB antenna dies. All ESP8266 pins are broken out on female headers (owner confirmed). Isolated on branch esp8266-uno-wifi-spike; main untouched. Test vehicle: uno-wifi-test.yaml — no wifi/api/ota/secrets, serial-only, GPIO5 RX / GPIO4 TX (only two non-strap interrupt-capable pins), and an every-15s Symphony loopback self-test using data=0x5A5 (deliberately NOT the fan's 0xD81) so it can never actuate the living-room fan. Pass = log shows the transmitted code decoded by the device's own receiver, mirroring the loopback behavior proven on the Feather 2026-08-09. ESP8266 caveat: bit-banged IR (no RMT), so this spike proves capability, not equivalence — an R1-style gate on real hardware still applies before trusting it.
notes: CORRECTION (roborev 3445, HIGH, verified in vendored source): on-device loopback is impossible on ESP8266 — remote_transmitter bit-bangs under InterruptLock (remote_transmitter.cpp:86-103) while remote_receiver captures via GPIO ISR (remote_receiver.cpp:74), so the device cannot hear its own TX. Test restructured to two legs: RX = point real fan remote at 5990, expect Received Symphony 0xD81; TX = 0x5A5 beacon every 15s, witnessed by a second receiver (Feather on ir-wiring-test.yaml or the prod living-room device's dump: all). Status: firmware flashed and booting on the HW-649 (DIP switches were hidden under factory kapton film; 5,6,7 to flash, 5,6 for logs); TX beacon confirmed firing in logs. Awaiting 5990 rewire + two-leg verification.
